summary: Three distribution lists for sending out Network documents such as RFCs, covering sites, the Network Information Center and station agents. These were postal addresses, not email lists. It replaced RFC 211 and was replaced by RFC 303.

plainLanguage.summary: An address book of who should get paper copies of network notes. It replaced an older one and was replaced again.

subtitle: Updated distribution lists for sending RFCs to ARPANET participants

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET continued to grow in early 1972, the distribution lists needed to be updated to include new sites and participants.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 300 updates RFC 211 with three revised mailing lists: List A for site liaisons, List B for other network participants and international contacts, and List C for NIC Station Agents.
tldr.outcome: This became the new standard distribution list and was replaced by RFC 303 as the network continued to expand.

today: RFC 300 is historic and obsoleted by RFC 303 as the ARPANET continued to grow. It is significant as evidence of the rapid expansion of network participation in the early 1970s, adding international sites and new institutions to the ARPANET community.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 300 was published in January 1972 and updates RFC 211. It provides three revised distribution lists for network documents. List A should be used by sites distributing their own documents to reach liaisons quickly. Lists B and C are used by the Network Information Center (NIC) to distribute to other participants and station agents respectively.

Like its predecessor, RFC 300 assumes postal delivery, recommending air mail for all but local deliveries. The RFC notes that phone numbers and site-specific information can be found in the Current Directory of Network Participants.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an updated phone book for sending network papers. It has new sites added since the last one.

sections.title: The Three Distribution Lists
sections.content:
List A (Initial Distribution) includes all network liaisons and others who should receive RFCs from either NIC or from sites. This list has expanded to include new sites like DOCB (Department of Commerce NOAA), UCSD-CC, and USAF-ETAC. It covers about 30 major network participants.

List B (NIC Distribution) consists of other network participants who receive all formal documents sent from NIC. This list includes international contacts such as NETH (Netherlands), UKICS (University of London), and WATERU (University of Waterloo in Canada).

List C (Station Agents) lists the local representatives at each site who distribute documents and receive a new mailing from NIC once a week or more frequently as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: List A is for the main people who need papers right away. List B includes people in other countries. List C is local helpers at each site.

sections.title: Network Expansion
sections.content:
RFC 300 reflects significant growth in the ARPANET since RFC 211. New sites have joined, including academic institutions like UCSD and University of Chicago, international research centers, and government agencies like USAF-ETAC and NOAA. The list shows the ARPANET's expansion from a primarily US-based network to one with international participation.

Despite the growth in participants, the distribution mechanism remains postal mail with air mail for distant sites. Each site is responsible for collecting its own mail and distributing documents internally through its station agent.
sections.plainLanguage: More universities and countries joined the network. The list is much longer now. But people still had to mail papers the old way.
